status_reason: A shortlist can be justified: the medium is aqueous and the targets are glucose and lactate, and the sources describe Raman for these metabolites in the same reactor and NIR for glucose in the millimolar range. The optical regime of the suspension and the required accuracy are unknown, so the NIR geometry stays conditional and the numbers for the go/no-go decision must come from the customer.

recommendations.rationale: Raman is the single method to test first: it is described for direct detection of specific metabolites such as glucose and lactate in the same reactor, and it tolerates an aqueous medium better than infrared methods. Its known weakness is a weak signal and possible fluorescence background, which is exactly what the trials must check on your medium.
recommendations.conditions: None beyond the general caveat that the Raman shift range and the excitation wavelength depend on the laser, spectrometer, fiber and probe actually selected.

citations.quote: Raman spectroscopy can be used in the same reactor to provide a "molecular fingerprint" for direct detection of specific metabolites like glucose, acetate, or lactate.
Raman is particularly well-suited for aqueous environments, as it exhibits low absorbance for water molecules compared to infrared methods.
measuring Raman spectra is hampered by the low intensity of Raman signals, which are several orders of magnitude weaker than IR absorption peaks

recommendations.rationale: NIR is the most common in-line fiber-probe method and is described as effective for glucose in the millimolar range. It applies only if the medium is transparent or semi-transparent enough for a controlled pathlength; if the suspension is too turbid or scattering, the geometry to test instead is diffuse reflection. Its broad overlapping bands require a chemometric model.
recommendations.conditions: Applies if the medium is optically clear or semi-transparent and a defined optical pathlength can be maintained. The 1-10 mm pathlength quoted from the source is a dairy example, not a value for your process.

citations.quote: Near-IR vibrational spectroscopy (NIR) is the most common online analysis method performed using fiber optic probes.
NIR spectroscopy is effective for tracking major components like glucose or glycerol in the millimolar range but may lack the sensitivity to detect trace compounds below 0.1 percent.
Transmission is the preferred method for transparent or semi-transparent liquids, such as skim milk, whey, or permeate.
it fails when the milk becomes too "thick" or fat-rich, as the light cannot penetrate the sample.
the precise control of the optical pathlength (usually 1 - 10 mm); if the pathlength is too wide, the signal is lost to absorption; if too narrow, the sample represents a negligible volume.
The broad absorption bands observed in this region overlap, suggesting the use of chemometrics for quantitative and qualitative analysis of spectral data.

recommendations.rationale: MIR ATR probes are described for in-line, in-process biotechnological environments, and their vibrational spectra carry information complementary to Raman. Run MIR ATR on its own as the comparison method first; the pairing with Raman is a later hypothesis of gain, to be tested only after the single-method results are in.
recommendations.conditions: Compare against the best single method (expected to be Raman) after the single-method tests. Treat any gain from the combination as a hypothesis, and align sampling location and timing.

Probe-based analysis is gaining widespread use in online analysis, such as in-line, in-process (chemical, biotechnological, natural) environments

strong absorption in the mid-IR region limits the corresponding spectral method to the analysis of very thin samples (usually less than 50 μm), but it opens up the possibility of using attenuated total reflectance (ATR)
suitability of analyzed samples for ATR measurements, which is true for liquid or soft solid samples and their components, allowing a tight contact with the probe head.

measurement_concept.probe_and_geometry: In-line, in-situ measurement with a fiber probe in the reactor or process line, with the spectrometers kept away from the process point. Raman: laser-excited fiber probe, contact measurement possible. NIR: transmission or transflection probe with a controlled pathlength if the medium is clear, or a flush-mounted diffuse-reflection probe if it is turbid. MIR: ATR probe whose crystal is in contact with the liquid.
measurement_concept.location: At the reactor or process line; the exact port, immersion depth and distance to the spectrometer are not yet known and depend on the answers to Q4.
measurement_concept.fiber_link: The fiber family must transmit the method's range. The sources state long cables (100-300 m) for low-OH silica fibers, which cover NIR and Raman, while MIR needs chalcogenide or polycrystalline fibers, and no achievable MIR link length is stated.

citations.quote: The use of these probes can be essential for in-situ analysis-in the field or in an ongoing process.
the probe is flush-mounted into a pipe or vat to interact directly with the flowing medium.
located safely away from the vibration and dust of the manufacturing floor.
Robust 100-300m cables made with Silica fibers of low OH-content (<0.1ppm OH) enable remote industrial process-control

spectral_ranges.statement: Raman shift in cm-1 is the spectral axis; the excitation wavelength is stated separately. The laser wavelength is not yet chosen. A source example uses 785 nm excitation, but this is an example, not a specification for your process.

risks.risk: The medium and the cell population change during the run. NIR and Raman calibrations are specific to the matrix, so a model built on part of the run may not hold for the rest of it, and will need re-validation or extension on new material.

Weak signal, fluorescence background; calibration specific to the matrix.

risks.risk: Probe contact and cleanliness: ATR needs tight contact and samples only a surface layer, so fouling or deposits on the crystal can bias results; on real samples Raman can be disturbed by a fluorescence background.
